newsitem.title: USA: US MUNICIPAL FOCUS - up but outpaced by Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: US MUNICIPAL FOCUS - up but outpaced by Treasuries.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond late on Friday gained one-half to three-quarters of a point, swept higher by the economy's surprising loss of 40,000 jobs in September, which jolted those who had predicted an increase.

However, the municipal bond market underperformed the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasuries, partly because buyers were fairly selective. While there were a number of bid wanted lists being circulated, as there have been all week, activity was not particularly brisk.

"There wasn't a large amount of...large blocks with good structure. The muni market was held back by that," a trader said. He noted that 10- to 15-year paper that is non-callable was among the types of issues for which there is demand.

However, supplies of such issues appeared to be fairly scarce in the secondary market, the trader said, explaining that issues that were callable, and had five- to seven-year maturities were more widely available.

Short-term issues sold earlier this week, like New York City's $1.6 billion Revenue Anticipation Notes, also benefited from the unexpected drop in the jobs, with yields falling around five basis points.
And at the long-end, a trader said some of the city's bonds, which offer an attractive structure, were bid up nearly one point.

Other actively quoted issues included Metropolitan Pier & Exposition Authority Illinois Dedicated State Tax Revenue Refunding of June 2027, which have a 5-1/4 percent coupon. They were bid at 5.72 percent, down eight basis points.
And Ohio State Turnpike Revenues of February 2026, which bear a coupon of 5-1/2 percent, were bid at 5.65 percent, down five basis points.

December municipal bond futures traded on the Chicago Board ended 1-1/32 higher at 116-9/32, while December U.S. Treasury bonds rose 1-12/32 to 111-22/32. The MOB spread eased to 147 ticks, reflecting some perceptions that municipals, whose premium to Treasuries a few weeks ago stood as high as the 170s, might have gotten a bit overpriced.

While a consensus survey of economists polled by Reuters showed they looked for the economy to have added 166,000 jobs in September, down from the previous month's revised rise of 235,000, the latest data instead showed a loss of 40,000.
This suggested to experts that the Federal Reserve, which late last month decided not to raise interest rates, likely will keep the same policy, at least for the near-term.
